property_summary: For any caller and value, on the correct contract SetMinSum(_val) always succeeds (does not revert) when the contract is not yet initialized and sets MinSum = _val; the mutant inverts the guard and will revert for those same inputs (preventing MinSum from being updated) when not initialized.

For any uint x, calling SetMinSum(x) on a fresh (not initialized) reference contract succeeds and sets MinSum to x; the mutant inverts the initialization guard causing SetMinSum to revert (and thus MinSum not updated) for those same inputs.

Once Initialized() has been called, SetMinSum must no longer change MinSum (i.e., SetMinSum reverts or fails to update MinSum); the mutant removed the guard so it allows MinSum to change after initialization.

For any input value x, calling SetMinSum(x) on the correct contract returns normally and updates MinSum to x; the mutant unconditionally reverts so a call to SetMinSum(x) will not succeed for some x (in fact for all x), breaking the rule that SetMinSum succeeds and sets MinSum to the provided value.

For any nonzero input value, calling SetMinSum(_val) on the correct contract sets MinSum to that value; the mutant refuses to accept zero (reverts) and thus for _val = 0 it leaves MinSum unchanged, so the mutant's behavior differs from the reference for some inputs.

For any input uint256 v, calling SetMinSum(v) on the reference C always results in MinSum == v (the contract accepts zero), whereas the mutant rejects v==0 causing MinSum to remain unchanged or the call to revert; the test fuzzes v and asserts that after SetMinSum(v) returns successfully, c.MinSum() equals v.

For every input _val, calling SetMinSum(_val) on the correct contract stores MinSum equal to the provided value _val; the mutant negates the assigned value (MinSum = ~_val) so for many _val the stored MinSum differs — the test asserts that c.MinSum() == _val after the call, which holds for reference but is violated by the mutant for some fuzzed _val.

For any caller and any uint _val, calling SetMinSum(_val) on the correct contract always leaves intitalized unchanged from false only if not previously initialized (i.e., SetMinSum does not flip intitalized to true); the mutant wrongly sets intitalized to true after SetMinSum for some inputs, causing subsequent SetMinSum calls to revert while the reference would allow them.

For all inputs, in the reference C calling SetLogFile(...) before Initialized() returns successfully and sets LogFile; the mutant inverts the guard so SetLogFile(...) reverts before Initialized() and only succeeds after Initialized(), violating that universal property.

Reference contract allows SetLogFile only before initialization; after Initialized() is called SetLogFile must revert, while the mutant (removed guard) will accept calls after initialization for some inputs.

In the reference, calling SetLogFile(address) does not permanently lock initialization (intitalized remains unchanged unless Initialized() is called), so calling SetLogFile multiple times by the same or different caller succeeds repeatedly; the mutant sets intitalized = true inside SetLogFile, making the second call revert — the test fuzzes two distinct caller addresses and a log address and asserts that two sequential SetLogFile calls both succeed on the reference but the mutant will cause at least some inputs to make the second call revert.

For any caller and log address, calling SetLogFile on the correct contract stores the provided Log address into the contract's LogFile state (accessible via the public getter) — the mutant instead fails to update LogFile and only calls AddMessage on the supplied log, so the stored LogFile remains unchanged for some inputs.

For any address supplied to SetLogFile before initialization, the reference contract stores that address into its LogFile state (so address(c.LogFile()) == supplied), whereas the mutant fails to update LogFile and therefore leaves address(c.LogFile()) unchanged (causing inequality for some inputs).

For any address supplied to SetLogFile before Initialized() is called, the reference contract stores that address as LogFile (so address(c.LogFile()) == supplied); the mutant instead does not set LogFile and merely calls AddMessage on the provided address, so address(c.LogFile()) != supplied for some inputs.

For any address X passed to SetLogFile before Initialized() is called, the reference contract stores X as its LogFile (so address(c.LogFile()) == X after the call); the mutant instead leaves LogFile unchanged for some X (it merely calls AddMessage on X), so address(c.LogFile()) != X for those inputs.

For any address L passed to SetLogFile before Initialized() is called, the reference implementation stores L into its LogFile state (so address(c.LogFile()) == L after the call), whereas the mutant that only calls AddMessage on L does not update LogFile, so address(c.LogFile()) != L for some inputs.

After calling SetLogFile(addr) from any caller, the reference contract always leaves intitalized == false until SetLogFile returns (so if the callee reenters and re-calls SetLogFile the reentry is blocked by the initial check), whereas the mutant sets intitalized true before assigning LogFile which can allow different revert/reentry effects and thus different external-visible outcomes; therefore the reference never observes SetLogFile reentrantly succeeding while the mutant can change that behavior for some callee that reenters.

For any caller and any Put(lock) call, the contract C never decreases that caller's stored unlockTime compared to its previous value (i.e., acc.unlockTime after Put >= previous acc.unlockTime); the mutant that unconditionally sets unlockTime = now+lock can decrease it for some inputs.

For any caller and any Put call, the contract never shortens that caller's unlockTime: after Put(...) completes, Acc[msg.sender].unlockTime >= prior unlockTime; the mutant that unconditionally sets unlockTime = now + _lockTime can make it smaller for some inputs.

For any caller and any Put call, the account's unlockTime after Put is either unchanged or increased to at least the new proposed absolute time (block.timestamp + _lockTime); the mutant that always sets unlockTime = block.timestamp + _lockTime can make the stored unlockTime strictly smaller than its previous value when _lockTime is small, violating monotonic non-decrease of unlockTime.

For any caller and any Put(_lockTime) the correct contract ensures that the stored unlockTime after Put is at least the caller's prior unlockTime unless the caller had zero balance and zero unlockTime (fresh account), while the mutant can reset an existing nonzero unlockTime to an earlier time when _lockTime is small.

For any account that already has a positive balance, calling Put with any _lockTime never decreases that account's unlockTime (i.e., after Put, unlockTime >= prior unlockTime); the mutant that unconditionally sets unlockTime = now + _lockTime can decrease it for some inputs where _lockTime is small, violating this rule.

For any caller and any payable Put(amount, lock) call, the contract preserves the caller's previous accumulated balance by adding msg.value to it (i.e., new balance >= previous balance and new balance == previous+msg.value); the mutant overwrites prior balance with msg.value, violating this for callers with non‑zero prior balance and non‑zero msg.value.

After calling Put with some msg.value, the holder's stored balance is always at least the msg.value greater than or equal to the previous balance (i.e. acc.balance_new == acc.balance_old + msg.value); the mutant that overwrites acc.balance with msg.value breaks this when acc.balance_old > 0 and msg.value > 0.

For any depositor and any nonnegative deposit, calling Put increases their stored balance to equal previous_balance + msg.value (i.e., acc.balance_new == acc.balance_old + msg.value); the mutant that overwrites acc.balance with msg.value breaks this when the depositor already had a nonzero prior balance and msg.value > 0.

For any caller and any nonzero deposit, calling Put increments that caller's stored Acc balance by the deposit amount (new_balance == old_balance + msg.value); the mutant that assigns acc.balance = msg.value breaks this when the caller already had a nonzero prior balance and msg.value > 0.

For any depositor and any nonnegative deposit and lock, calling Put increments their stored Acc balance (new_balance == old_balance + msg.value); the mutant that sets acc.balance = msg.value can violate this when the depositor already has a nonzero prior balance and msg.value > 0.

For any caller, after calling Put(...) with some nonzero msg.value the reference contract always records a Log.History entry (i.e., increases History length / LastMsg) for that Put, whereas the mutant that removed the logging will not increase the log for some inputs (nonzero value).

For any caller and lockTime, calling Put with msg.value == 0 is accepted by the reference contract and leaves acc.balance unchanged but still updates unlockTime and emits/logs the Put call; the mutant reverts on msg.value == 0, breaking this universal acceptance for some inputs.

For any caller and any lockTime, calling Put with zero ether does NOT revert on the reference and thus the call succeeds (allowing unlockTime to update and a log entry); the mutant reverts when msg.value == 0, breaking this rule for such inputs.

For any caller and any lockTime, calling Put(...) with zero ETH should succeed on the reference contract (not revert) and thus a zero-value Put call is accepted; the mutant inserts a revert on msg.value==0 so it will reject some zero-value Put calls and thus violate this rule.

For any caller and any lockTime, calling Put(...) with zero ETH should succeed (not revert) on the reference C and thus return ok=true; the mutant reverts when msg.value==0 so for some fuzzed (caller, lockTime, amount=0) the mutant makes the call fail and ok=false.

For any caller and any lockTime, calling Put(...) with a nonzero msg.value either increases the caller's recorded balance by that msg.value (and succeeds); the mutant that reverts on msg.value==0 still preserves this for nonzero values but would reject zero-value puts — so we assert that when msg.value > 0 the call succeeds and increases Acc[caller].balance by msg.value.

For any caller and any nonnegative lockTime, calling Put with zero value is allowed by the reference (it does not revert) and leaves contract state unchanged w.r.t. balance for that caller, whereas the mutant requires msg.value>0 and thus reverts for zero-value calls, breaking that rule.

For any caller and any lockTime, calling Put with zero value does not revert on the reference and leaves the caller's recorded balance unchanged; the mutant instead reverts for msg.value == 0, breaking this rule for zero-value calls.

For any caller and any lockTime, calling Put with any nonnegative msg.value never decreases the caller's recorded acc.balance (i.e., acc.balance after Put is >= acc.balance before), while the mutant that requires msg.value>0 can make zero-value calls revert and thus violate the universal property that Put never reverts for msg.value==0 and leaves balances non-decreasing for all inputs.

For any caller and any lockTime, calling Put with msg.value == 0 always succeeds on the reference and leaves the caller's recorded balance unchanged; the mutant requires msg.value > 0 and thus will revert for some zero-value calls, violating this rule.

For any caller and any lockTime, calling Put with msg.value == 0 on the reference contract always succeeds and leaves the caller's recorded balance unchanged; the mutant requires msg.value > 0 and thus will revert for some zero-value calls, breaking this rule.

For any caller, when block.timestamp equals the stored unlockTime the correct contract C disallows Collect (withdrawal) (requires strictly greater), whereas the mutant that uses >= allows withdrawal at exactly unlockTime; the test places funds and sets unlockTime then checks that Collect is rejected at exact unlockTime.

For any depositor and amounts, if Collect is invoked exactly at the stored unlockTime then the reference contract rejects the withdrawal (Collect reverts/does not send), while the mutant (using >=) would allow a successful withdrawal at that exact timestamp.

For any depositor and amount, if Collect is invoked at a timestamp exactly equal to the stored unlockTime, the reference contract rejects the withdrawal (Collect does not send funds), whereas the mutant using >= would allow the withdrawal at that exact timestamp.

For any depositor and amount, if Collect is called exactly at the stored unlockTime and the external recipient reverts on receive, the reference C will NOT reduce the contract balance (Collect will not send funds) while the mutant (>=) can attempt the send and thus may observe a difference; the test asserts that calling Collect at unlockTime never succeeds in sending funds (address(c).balance unchanged) on the reference but the mutant can differ.

For any depositor and amount, calling Collect exactly at the stored unlockTime always fails (Collect does not transfer funds) in the correct C (strict >), while the mutant using >= can succeed at that timestamp and thus change contract balance.

For any caller and amount, a successful call to Collect only occurs when the holder's balance is >= the requested amount (so after Collect returns the stored balance is original minus amount); the mutant removes that pre-check and can cause Collect to revert or behave inconsistently for some inputs (e.g., when _am > acc.balance).

For every caller and amounts, if Collect(...) returns (does not revert) then the contract's stored balance for that caller decreases by exactly the requested amount and address(c).balance decreases accordingly; the mutant can either revert or violate this by attempting to subtract more than the stored balance, causing a different observable outcome for some inputs.

For any caller, if Collect(amount) returns successfully then the caller's stored balance (Acc(caller).balance) is decreased by exactly amount and address(c).balance decreased accordingly; the mutant that removes the acc.balance>=_am check can cause Collect to revert or not satisfy this (e.g., when amount > balance), so there exist inputs where this property fails.

For all callers, if Collect(...) returns (does not revert) then acc.balance after the call equals the prior balance minus the requested _am (i.e., balances only decrease by the withdrawn amount); the mutant that removes the acc.balance>=_am check can cause Collect to revert or otherwise violate this by attempting to subtract more than the stored balance for some inputs.

For any caller, whenever Collect(amount) returns successfully the contract's stored holder balance for that caller is decreased by exactly amount (i.e., Acc(caller).balance_new = Acc(caller).balance_old - amount); the mutant that removes the check allowing Collect to proceed when amount > balance will sometimes cause Collect to revert (or otherwise not satisfy this observable decrease), so this universal property holds on the reference but is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

Invariant: A successful Collect call on behalf of an account always decreases that account's recorded balance by the withdrawn amount; the mutant that moves the balance update after the external call can leave the recorded balance unchanged if the external send fails, breaking this rule for some inputs (failing callee).

For any caller and amount where Collect is allowed, a successful Collect call always reduces the caller's recorded acc.balance by the withdrawn amount; the mutant that moves the balance update after the external call can leave acc.balance unchanged when the external transfer fails, so a failing callee breaks this rule.
